title: postfix ! is accepted inside a labeled statement's block, which is an ordinary statement position
notes: specification/failures.mdx, 'Accepted Placements': 'A `!` on a Result operand MUST be accepted if and only if all five hold', condition 1 being that every enclosing node out to the nearest statement or arrow function is one of exactly seven forms. The `!` here is the initializer of a single-declarator variable statement, which is condition 1's sixth form, and the walk stops at that statement immediately. A label wraps a statement; it does not put the declaration into an expression position, so nothing about it can change the placement verdict. This is the ONE row in the 2026-08-25 divergence set where the Go fork is right and the JS reference is wrong, which is why it is written from the rule and marked against the reference rather than the other way round. RETIRED XFAIL (js). THE MARKER'S STATED CAUSE WAS WRONG, and worth recording because it would have sent the next reader to the wrong file: it said the reference lowered the guard AROUND the label rather than into it. Dumping the lowering shows the guard already inside the labeled block, correctly. The real defect was one statement further down — `statementMayFallThrough` had arms for `return`, `throw`, block, if/else, `switch` and `try` and NO arm for a labeled statement, so it defaulted to "may complete normally", `implicitCompletion` appended `return __vsResultSuccess(undefined)` after a `return` that always runs, and the stock emitted-module check rejected the lowered program with TS2322 — a program the placement rule ACCEPTS, lowered into TypeScript that cannot be checked. Nothing about the placement rule was touched. THE CLASS WAS MEASURED and this case was one of four members, the only one the corpus registered: `while (true) { … return … }`, `for (;;) { … return … }` and `outer: inner: { … return … }` each produced the same TS2322 on the reference while the fork ran them and printed, and all four agree after the one edit. The unconditional-loop arms are conditioned on `break`, counted rather than resolved to a target: over-approximating re-adds a dead statement, which is safe, while under-approximating would drop a completion — and that direction is self-checking, since a function that really can run off its end is refused by the emitted-module check's own "not all code paths return a value" rather than accepted silently.
